Create a GPU table: a data frame in GPU memory

Source: R/tbl-gpu.R
tbl_gpu.Rd

tbl_gpu() copies an R data frame to GPU memory and returns a tbl_gpu, cuplyr's GPU table. You work with it as with a tibble: pipe it through dplyr verbs such as filter(), mutate(), summarise() or left_join(), which run on the GPU, and bring the result back to R with collect().

Usage

tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'data.frame'
tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
tbl_gpu(data, ..., lazy = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble to transfer to GPU memory. Supported column types are double, integer, bit64::integer64, character, logical, factor, Date and POSIXct (see "Column types" below).

...

Additional arguments passed to methods (currently unused).

lazy

Logical or character. Controls execution mode:

  • TRUE or "lazy" - Operations are deferred until collect()/compute()

  • FALSE or "eager" - Operations execute immediately

  • NULL (default) - Use the session option, then the environment variable, then the package default, which is lazy

The default can be changed with options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager") or the environment variable CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=eager; the argument beats the option, which beats the variable. An invalid option value warns once and the default is used. All options are listed on cuplyr-options.

Value

A GPU table: an object of class tbl_gpu that holds the data in GPU memory and works with dplyr verbs. Use collect() to get a tibble back.

Details

The data is copied to GPU memory as soon as tbl_gpu() is called (also in lazy mode; only the verbs are deferred). The GPU memory is freed when the R object is garbage collected.

Working with a GPU table

A tbl_gpu works with the dplyr verbs. What the GPU can't do, dplyr does on the CPU, and the result comes back to the GPU as a tbl_gpu (see cuplyr-fallback to be told when that happens).

  • collect() runs the pending steps and brings the result back to R as a tibble (a plain data.frame if you uploaded one).

  • compute() runs the pending steps and keeps the result on the GPU, as a tbl_gpu with nothing pending: use it for a result you use more than once.

  • explain() and show_query() print the pending plan, one dplyr call per step, without running it.

  • print() and glimpse() show the dimensions, the column types and the first rows.

Lazy and eager execution

A tbl_gpu is lazy by default: each verb adds a step to a plan, and the GPU does the work when a result is needed: collect(), compute(), printing, nrow()/dim(), pull() or $. A few steps need the result of the pending plan as soon as they are called, and run it then, on the GPU (see "Plan breaks" in cuplyr-fallback). Before a plan runs, cuplyr optimizes it: columns no later step reads are dropped early, consecutive mutate() calls are combined, filter() conditions move closer to the data (below a mutate() they don't depend on, or into an input of a join when that can't change the join's result, errors or warnings, for example below a cross join or a join with relationship = "many-to-many"), and of several filter() calls in a row the cheaper conditions run first.

Errors in a verb's arguments (a missing column, a type error) are still raised when the verb is called. Printing a lazy table with pending operations (or calling glimpse() on it) runs the plan to show its first rows, under a # A tbl_gpu [lazy]: header; the table itself is unchanged and nothing is kept, so printing it twice runs the plan twice (compute() it first to look at it repeatedly). If the plan fails (an error, out of GPU memory), the print shows the schema and the message instead of raising.

In eager mode (tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)), each dplyr verb runs on the GPU at once. This is simple but can lead to unnecessary intermediate allocations. options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager") (or the environment variable CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=eager) makes every new tbl_gpu eager, and as_eager() and as_lazy() switch one table.

For measured timings and memory use of the two modes, see vignette("performance", package = "cuplyr").

Column types

Each R column type is stored as a GPU type, the type the table's schema shows:

  • numeric (double) -> FLOAT64

  • integer -> INT32

  • bit64::integer64 -> INT64, exact. collect() gives a bit64::integer64 back (a double, with a warning past 2^53, when bit64 is not installed).

  • character -> STRING

  • logical -> BOOL8

  • factor (ordered too) -> DICTIONARY32: the integer codes are on the GPU and the levels stay in R, so collect() gives the factor back with the same levels.

  • Date -> TIMESTAMP_DAYS

  • POSIXct -> TIMESTAMP_MICROSECONDS, the instant in UTC on the GPU with the time zone kept alongside, so collect() gives the same zone back.

A vctrs::unspecified() column (all NA, no type yet) is stored as BOOL8. It collects back as vctrs::unspecified() only while it passes through filter(), arrange(), slice() and semi_join()/anti_join() (as a column of x, as in dplyr); every other verb (select(), mutate(), group_by() with computed expressions, slice_min()/slice_max(), a mutating join, vctrs::vec_slice()) returns it as a plain logical column. An all-NA logical or unspecified column joins a string, Date, POSIXct or factor key, as in dplyr: a merged key takes that key's type; with keep = TRUE, in a non-equi condition and in semi_join()/anti_join() each key column keeps its own type. A logical key with a value in it errors. Bound to a character column in bind_rows(), an unspecified column errors.

A matrix column with more than one column (or more than two dimensions), a list column, a data frame column and a complex or raw column have no GPU form: tbl_gpu() raises cuplyr_error_unsupported_class naming the column. A verb that ran on the CPU and returned a matrix or array raises cuplyr_error_unsupported_result_class the same way; one that returned a list or data frame column hands back a plain tibble.

Dates and times the GPU can't hold

A GPU Date holds whole days in an int32 and a POSIXct holds int64 microseconds. A value that doesn't fit becomes NA when it is uploaded, with a warning:

  • cuplyr_warning_infinite_timestamp: Inf or -Inf.

  • cuplyr_warning_timestamp_out_of_range: a finite value beyond about 5.8 million years either side of 1970 (Date) or 292,000 years (POSIXct).

Both also inherit cuplyr_warning_timestamp_unrepresentable, so one handler covers both. An upload raises at most one warning per class, listing every affected column with its count, e.g. `d` (2 values), `t` (1 value). NA and NaN are ordinary missing values and never warn. The same applies to every other way values reach the GPU: copy = TRUE joins, bind_rows(), $<-, a constant in mutate(), and the result of a verb that ran on the CPU. A fractional Date is floored with its own warning, cuplyr_warning_fractional_date.

See also

collect.tbl_gpu to transfer data back to R, compute.tbl_gpu to execute and keep on GPU, explain.tbl_gpu and show_query.tbl_gpu to see the plan, filter.tbl_gpu, mutate.tbl_gpu, select.tbl_gpu for data manipulation

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  # Transfer mtcars to GPU (lazy by default)
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)
  print(gpu_mtcars)

  # Operations are deferred until collect()
  result <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
    filter(mpg > 20) |>
    mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425) |>
    collect()

  # Eager mode: each verb runs at once
  eager_tbl <- tbl_gpu(mtcars, lazy = FALSE)

  # Or make every new table eager:
  # options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager")
}
